title: System design: scaling and architecture
tagline: Scaling up and out, balancing load, drawing service boundaries, and checking a design with numbers before it is built.
why: Many production puzzles are design consequences: a session kept in one server's memory, a health check that tests nothing, a split into services that now must ship together. When you can see the design behind a symptom, you stop debugging one instance and fix the shape. You will also be asked to judge designs for AI products, and a few checked numbers settle most of those arguments.
objectives: Name the state that stops an app server from being copied, and say where to move it
Explain why one instance can receive most of the traffic, and name the balancer setting to check
Tell a modular monolith from a distributed monolith by how its releases are coordinated
Estimate peak requests per second, open streams, tokens, and storage for an LLM chat product from user counts
Name the tradeoff made at each step of a data path and say what breaks first at ten times the load

lessons.title: Scaling up vs scaling out, and statelessness

blocks.text: **Scaling up** (vertical scaling) means giving one machine more CPU, memory, or faster disks. **Scaling out** (horizontal scaling) means running more copies of a service behind a load balancer. Scaling up is simpler and changes no code. Scaling out has no fixed ceiling, but it only works when any copy can handle any request.

That last condition is the whole lesson. A copy can handle any request only if the process keeps nothing between requests that the next request needs. This property is called **statelessness**. The state still exists. It lives in Postgres, Redis, or object storage instead of inside the process.

options.name: Scale up
gain: No code or architecture change
One process to debug
Memory and local disk keep working as before
cost: A hard ceiling at the largest machine
One machine is one failure
Resizing usually means a restart
options.choose: Choose this when the load fits on one machine with room to spare, or when the service holds state that is hard to move, such as a database primary.

options.name: Scale out
gain: Capacity grows by adding copies
One copy can die without an outage
Copies can follow the load up and down
cost: Every piece of local state must move out first
Needs a load balancer and health checks
Bugs now depend on which copy served the request
options.choose: Choose this for stateless app servers and workers, which is most of what Relay runs.

blocks.text: State that hides in an app server

blocks.caption: Local state and what it does once there are two copies
rows: Users logged out when a request lands on another copy
Redis or Postgres, keyed by a session ID
A file uploaded to one copy returns 404 from the others
A module-level dict or LRU cache
Copies disagree, so a change appears and disappears
Redis, or accept short staleness per copy
A timer started inside each process
The nightly email goes out once per copy
One scheduler, or a lock only one copy can hold
A random key generated at startup
Cookies signed by one copy are rejected by another
One shared secret from the secret manager
The real limit is the configured one times the number of copies
blocks.verdict: Walk this table before adding a second copy of any service. Each row is a bug that only exists once there are two.

blocks.title: The second copy is the real test
blocks.text: A service that has only ever run as one process is not known to be stateless. These bugs pass every test on a laptop and appear the day an autoscaler adds a copy, which is usually the day traffic is highest.

blocks.q: Relay's API ran as one instance for months. After scaling to three behind round robin, about two thirds of screenshot links that customers upload come back broken. What is the most likely cause?
options: Uploads are written to the local disk of whichever instance received them
The CDN is serving a stale copy of each image
The database lost the rows that reference the images
blocks.explain: Two thirds is the chance that the image request reaches one of the two instances that do not hold the file. Moving uploads to object storage lets any instance serve any file.

blocks.text: When to add copies: autoscaling signals

An **autoscaler** adds or removes copies when a chosen metric crosses a threshold. The metric must rise when users start to suffer. If it does not, the autoscaler reacts to the wrong thing or never reacts at all.

blocks.caption: Signals an autoscaler can follow
rows: The service mostly waits on I/O, so CPU stays low while users queue
Copies are busy for any reason
A slow dependency fills every copy, and more copies only add load to it
Failing jobs are retried and inflate the queue
It lags the cause, and a slow database raises it on every copy at once
blocks.verdict: For I/O-bound services such as Relay's API, scale on requests in flight, and cap the maximum so the autoscaler cannot overwhelm Postgres or the LLM quota.

blocks.title: LLM calls keep CPU near idle
blocks.text: A Relay chat request spends most of its time waiting for model tokens. One copy can hold many open streams while its CPU stays low, so a CPU-based autoscaler may never fire. Scale on concurrent requests, and remember that every copy you add shares the same provider tokens-per-minute limit.

blocks.title: Scaling out made it worse
blocks.text: If adding copies raised errors, look downstream. Each copy opens its own database pool, so ten copies with pools of 20 ask Postgres for 200 connections. Check the database's connection count and the provider's rate-limit headers before adding more copies.

blocks.prompt: An autoscaler doubles Relay's API copies during a traffic spike, and p95 latency gets worse. Which resources do you check first, and why?
blocks.answer: The ones every copy shares: Postgres connections and the LLM provider's rate limit. More copies send more concurrent work to the same bottleneck, so the queue moves from the API to the database or the provider, where it is slower and harder to see.

blocks.text: A **load balancer** receives each request or connection and picks one healthy backend copy to handle it. Two questions define it: how much of the traffic it reads before choosing, and what rule it uses to choose. Both decide how evenly load spreads and which failures it can hide from you.

blocks.caption: Layer 4 and layer 7 balancing
rows: Carry any protocol at very high throughput
Route by path, terminate TLS, add headers, retry
One long connection pins all of its requests to one backend
Parses every request, adding work and another set of timeouts
Non-HTTP traffic, or raw throughput at the edge
HTTP APIs such as nginx in front of Relay's FastAPI service
blocks.verdict: Prefer layer 7 for HTTP services so that balancing happens per request. Use layer 4 for non-HTTP protocols or when throughput matters more than routing.

blocks.text: Choosing a backend

items: **Round robin** sends to each backend in turn. Even when requests cost about the same, uneven when some take 50 ms and others take 30 seconds.
**Least connections** sends to the backend with the fewest open requests. Better when cost varies, such as LLM streams of very different lengths.
**Hashing on a key** maps the same user or key to the same backend every time. Good for cache locality, skewed when a few keys are very hot.
**Consistent hashing** is a hashing scheme in which adding or removing one of N backends moves only about 1/N of the keys, instead of nearly all of them.

blocks.q: Relay's API serves quick order lookups and chat streams that last up to 40 seconds, balanced round robin. Some copies hold 400 open requests while others hold 30. Which change spreads load best?
options: Switch the balancer to least connections
Add more copies and keep round robin
Hash on the customer ID
blocks.explain: Round robin counts turns, not work, so a copy that happens to receive many long streams still gets its full share of new requests. Least connections sends new work to the least busy copy. More copies under round robin keep the same imbalance.

blocks.text: Health checks and sticky sessions

A **health check** is a request the balancer sends to each backend on a schedule. Backends that fail it stop receiving traffic. The check proves only what it tests. A `/healthz` handler that returns 200 without touching anything proves that the process can answer HTTP, and nothing else.

blocks.title: nginx in front of Relay's API, the parts that decide balancing
notes: `least_conn` picks the backend with the fewest active connections. Without it, nginx uses round robin.
`max_fails` and `fail_timeout` are passive checks: open-source nginx marks a backend unavailable after failed attempts in real traffic and does not send probe requests of its own.
By default only connection errors and timeouts count as failed attempts. A backend that answers every request with a fast 500 stays in rotation.
`proxy_read_timeout` is the longest silence allowed between two reads from the backend; the default is 60 seconds. `proxy_buffering off` lets streamed tokens through as they arrive.

blocks.title: What the health check should test

options.name: Shallow check
gain: A shared outage never removes every copy
Cheap and fast
cost: Passes while the copy cannot do real work
A broken copy keeps receiving its share of traffic
options.choose: Choose this for liveness, the question of whether the process should be restarted.

options.name: Deep check on shared dependencies
gain: Removes copies that cannot reach Postgres or Redis
cost: A database blip fails every copy at once
The balancer is left with no backends
Adds a query per check
options.choose: Choose this rarely, and only when sending traffic to a copy that cannot reach the dependency is worse than refusing everyone.

options.name: Check of local resources
gain: Catches faults in one copy, such as an exhausted connection pool
Does not fail every copy for one shared blip
cost: More code in the handler
Can still miss a broken code path
options.choose: Choose this for readiness, for example by taking a pool connection within a short timeout.

blocks.text: **Sticky sessions** (session affinity) make the balancer send a user back to the same backend each time, usually by setting a cookie. They hide state left in an app server instead of removing it. When that backend restarts, is replaced in a deploy, or is removed by the autoscaler, its users lose whatever it held.

options.name: Sticky sessions
gain: No new infrastructure
Works with state already in memory
cost: Users logged out when their backend goes away
Uneven load when some users are much heavier
Every deploy disrupts sessions
options.choose: Choose this as a stopgap, or when per-user state is expensive to rebuild and losing it now and then is acceptable.

options.name: External session store
gain: Any copy can serve any user
Deploys and scale-in keep sessions
cost: A Redis or database read on each request
One more dependency that can fail
options.choose: Choose this as the default for any service that runs more than one copy.

blocks.title: One instance receives most of the traffic
blocks.text: Check in this order: long-lived connections (keep-alive, HTTP/2, WebSockets, SSE) still attached to copies that existed before a scale-out; sticky sessions with a few heavy users; a layer 4 balancer in front of multiplexed connections; clients that cached one DNS answer. If the imbalance stays after new copies join, connections are pinned.

blocks.title: An API gateway is a layer 7 balancer with opinions
blocks.text: An **API gateway** is a reverse proxy that also authenticates, rate limits, and routes paths to different services. nginx in front of Relay plays a small version of this role. Each feature it takes on is one more place a request can be refused before your code sees it.

blocks.prompt: A health check runs a query against Postgres. Postgres fails over and is unreachable for 20 seconds. What does the load balancer do, and what do users see?
blocks.answer: Every copy fails its check at about the same time, so the balancer marks all backends unhealthy and users get errors from the balancer itself, often 502 or 503. A 20 second database blip becomes a full outage at the front door, and lasts longer if copies need several passing checks to return.

blocks.text: A **monolith** is one deployable unit that holds all of an application's code. **Microservices** split the application into separately deployed services that talk over the network. A **modular monolith** is one deployable unit with strict internal boundaries, where modules talk only through defined interfaces. Relay is one API service and one worker fleet, which is close to a monolith.

blocks.caption: Three ways to organize the same product
rows: Each service on its own schedule
A function call through a defined interface
A network call that can time out
One database, tables owned by modules
A database per service, no cross-service joins
Owners per service, contracts between them
A change anywhere can break everything
blocks.verdict: Start with a monolith, keep it modular, and split out a service when one part needs a different scale, release cadence, failure tolerance, or owning team.

blocks.text: Splitting does not remove complexity. It turns function calls into network calls, and each one gains latency, a timeout, a retry policy, and a way to fail partially. Every failure mode from day 18 becomes possible inside your own product.

blocks.title: Should the agent loop leave Relay's API?

options.name: Keep it in the API
gain: One deploy, one trace, one log stream
A change across the boundary is a normal code change
cost: The agent's heavy dependencies ship with every API change
Cannot scale the agent apart from order pages
options.choose: Choose this while one team owns both parts and they grow together.

options.name: Separate agent service
gain: Scales and deploys on its own schedule
An agent crash leaves login and order pages up
cost: A network hop with its own timeout and retries
A versioned contract to keep compatible
Two places to look for every bug
options.choose: Choose this when the agent has a different load shape, failure tolerance, or owning team.

blocks.text: Service boundaries and discovery

A good boundary lets two services change and deploy without asking each other. It usually follows a business capability, such as billing or search, and the service owns its own data. A bad boundary splits one workflow across services that must change together. The result is a **distributed monolith**: every cost of microservices with none of the independence.

blocks.title: A deploy needs five services released in order
blocks.text: That release plan is the signature of a distributed monolith. The services share a contract that cannot change compatibly, or they share database tables. The fix is a boundary that matches how the code actually changes, or contracts that stay backward compatible so each service can ship alone.

**Service discovery** is how one service finds the current addresses of another. In Kubernetes it is a stable DNS name in front of changing pod addresses. Elsewhere it may be a registry such as Consul. When discovery is stale, calls go to copies that no longer exist and fail with connection refused or timeouts.

blocks.q: Relay's team split billing into its own service. Now every API release also needs a billing release in a fixed order, or refunds fail. What does this suggest most strongly?
options: The boundary cuts across a workflow that changes as one unit
Billing needs more replicas to keep up with the API
Service discovery is returning stale billing addresses
blocks.explain: Lockstep releases mean the two services cannot change independently, which was the point of splitting them. Replicas and discovery are runtime concerns, and neither forces an order on releases.

blocks.text: A second boundary question is whether to own a component at all. Queues, databases, search, auth, and model hosting can each be built and run by your team or bought as a managed service.

options.name: Buy a managed service
gain: Running in days instead of months
Patching, backups, and failover handled for you
cost: Less control over limits, versions, and outage timing
Cost grows with usage
Leaving later takes work
options.choose: Choose this for anything that is not the product's advantage, such as Relay's database, queue, and model API.

options.name: Build it yourself
gain: Exact fit to your access pattern
No per-use fees or vendor limits
cost: Your team owns every outage and upgrade
Months before it is as reliable as the bought one
options.choose: Choose this when the component is the product's advantage, or when usage makes the bought version clearly worse or more expensive.

blocks.title: Agent tools are service contracts
blocks.text: Each tool Relay's agent can call, such as `lookup_order`, is a contract between the model and your backend. Renaming an argument is a breaking change for every prompt and eval case that uses the tool, and deserves the same compatibility care as a public API.

blocks.title: Debugging across a split
blocks.text: Once a request crosses services, a log search in one service shows half the story. Make sure a request ID travels in a header through every hop and appears in every log line, or you will be matching timestamps by hand.

blocks.prompt: A teammate proposes splitting Relay into eight services to make it easier to debug. What would you ask before agreeing?
blocks.answer: Which part needs to scale, deploy, or fail separately, and who will own each service. If nothing differs in load, release cadence, or ownership, the split adds network calls, distributed traces, and version skew, all of which make debugging harder. Clear module boundaries inside one service give most of the clarity at far lower cost.

blocks.text: A design review follows a procedure. You state what the system must do, put rough numbers on it, draw the path of the main request, find what saturates first, and make each choice with its cost named. This lesson walks that procedure for the backend of a general LLM chat product, larger than Relay.

items: **Requirements.** What users do, plus targets such as time to first token, availability, and how long conversations are kept.
**Numbers.** Users to requests per second, then peak, then concurrency, tokens, and storage. Orders of magnitude are enough.
**Data path.** One request from the browser to storage and back, with every hop named.
**Bottleneck.** The resource that saturates first as load grows.
**Choices.** At each step, the option picked and what it costs.
**Ten times.** What breaks first if the numbers grow tenfold, and what you would measure.

blocks.text: Back-of-envelope numbers

Assume 1 million daily active users, each sending 10 messages a day. Each turn sends the conversation so far, averaging 2,000 input tokens, and the model replies with about 300 output tokens. Peak traffic is three times the daily average. These are assumptions, and you state them out loud so others can challenge them.

blocks.title: The arithmetic, checked
blocks.code:
messages per day     1,000,000 users x 10              = 10,000,000
average rate         10,000,000 / 86,400 s             ~ 116 per second
peak rate            116 x 3                           ~ 350 per second

stream duration      ~1 s to first token + 300 tokens at ~50 per s  ~ 7 s
open streams (peak)  350 per second x 7 s              ~ 2,500 at once

input tokens (peak)  350 x 2,000                       ~ 700,000 per second
output tokens (peak) 350 x 300                         ~ 105,000 per second
input per day        10,000,000 x 2,000                = 20 billion

stored per exchange  user text + reply + metadata      ~ 2 KB
storage per day      10,000,000 x 2 KB                 ~ 20 GB
storage per year     20 GB x 365                       ~ 7 TB
database writes      350 x 2 rows                      ~ 700 inserts per second
notes: Open streams equal arrival rate times duration, which is **Little's law**. About 2,500 streams open at once sizes connection handling, not CPU.
Input tokens dwarf output tokens because every turn resends the history. Trimming or summarizing history is the largest lever on cost and on the provider's tokens-per-minute limit.
700 inserts per second is a moderate load for one Postgres primary. Seven terabytes a year is the number that forces a retention decision.
The token rates are the first hard wall. They must fit under the provider's limits for your account at peak, not on average.

blocks.title: One chat turn through the backend

steps.label: Sends the message and opens a stream
steps.detail: The browser posts the new message and keeps the response open as server-sent events, so tokens appear as they are generated.
steps.fail: A proxy that buffers responses delivers the whole reply at the end, and the product feels frozen.

steps.label: Picks an API copy by least connections
steps.detail: Streams last seconds, so least connections spreads open streams evenly. Idle timeouts are raised above the longest expected silence.
steps.fail: A long pause before the first token trips the idle timeout, and the client sees the stream close with no reply.

steps.label: Authenticates and checks the user's budget
steps.detail: The session and a per-user token budget live in Redis, so any copy can serve the turn.
steps.fail: If Redis is down, the API must choose between failing open and failing closed on the budget.

steps.label: Saves the user message, loads history
steps.detail: The user message is written before the model is called, so a later crash cannot lose it. History is read by conversation ID and time, which one composite index serves.
steps.fail: Without that index the history read becomes a scan that slows as the table grows.

steps.label: Generates the reply as a stream
steps.detail: The API calls the provider with the trimmed history and relays tokens to the browser as they arrive.
steps.fail: 429 or overload errors at peak, and a slow first token when the prompt is long.

steps.label: Saves the finished reply
steps.detail: The reply and its token counts are written when the stream ends, with a status of complete, stopped, or failed.
steps.fail: If the user closes the tab, the API must decide whether to finish and save the reply or cancel and stop paying for tokens.

steps.label: Runs follow-up work off the request
steps.detail: Conversation titles, moderation, usage accounting, and search indexing go through the job queue so they never delay the reply.
steps.fail: Queue lag shows as missing titles or late usage numbers, not as slow chat.

blocks.caption: The choice made at each step
rows: Long-lived connections; every proxy timeout must be tuned
Held by the API, never sent to the browser
All traffic passes through us, so we carry every open stream
Recent turns plus a running summary
Cheaper and faster; the model can lose details from early turns
Simple queries; old partitions must be archived or dropped
Results arrive later; one more system to watch
Pay per token and live within rate limits; no GPUs to run
blocks.verdict: Each row trades some quality, freshness, or control for cost and simplicity. Write each assumption next to its number, and say each trade out loud, so both can be revisited when the numbers change.

blocks.title: Where this design breaks first
blocks.text: At ten times the load the provider limit fails before anything you run: about 7 million input tokens per second at peak. Watch time to first token, 429 counts from the provider, open streams per API copy, and the growth of the message table. Each maps to one row of the choice table.

blocks.title: Answering with components instead of numbers
blocks.text: A design that lists Kafka, a vector database, and five services before any number is computed is a memorized answer. At 350 requests per second, a stateless API, one Postgres primary, Redis, and a queue can carry the first version. The numbers tell you where complexity is worth paying for.

blocks.q: Product wants to double the history sent with each turn to improve answers. Using the numbers above, which resource does this affect most?
options: Input tokens, and with them cost, first-token latency, and the rate limit
Database storage, because each stored message doubles in size
Open streams, because each stream lasts twice as long
Database writes, because each turn writes twice as many rows
blocks.explain: History is resent as input on every turn, so doubling it roughly doubles input tokens, which drive cost, the tokens-per-minute limit, and time to first token. Stored messages keep their size, and output length, which sets stream duration, does not change.

blocks.prompt: Redo the numbers for 30 messages per user per day instead of 10. Which numbers change, and which decisions are most affected?
blocks.answer: Everything triples: about 1,050 requests per second at peak, about 7,500 open streams, 2.1 million input tokens per second, and about 22 TB of messages a year. The provider rate limit and the retention policy are hit hardest. The stateless API simply runs more copies.

fieldGuide.symptom: Users randomly logged out, more often since the service runs on several instances
causes: Sessions kept in one instance's memory
Each instance signs cookies with its own key generated at startup
Sticky sessions lost when an instance restarts or scales in
fieldGuide.look: Which instance served each request that lost its session, and whether the session record still exists in the store.
fieldGuide.confirm: Lost sessions cluster on particular instances, or start right after a scale-out or deploy.
fieldGuide.fix: Move sessions to Redis or Postgres and load one shared signing secret on every instance. This costs a store read per request.

fieldGuide.symptom: One instance receives most of the traffic
causes: Long-lived connections still attached to instances that existed before a scale-out
Sticky sessions with a few heavy users
Round robin with requests of very different cost
fieldGuide.look: Requests and open connections per instance in the balancer's metrics, and the balancing algorithm in its configuration.
fieldGuide.confirm: The imbalance follows connections or keys rather than instance capacity, and stays after new instances join.
fieldGuide.fix: Use least connections, cap connection lifetime so clients reconnect, or remove stickiness. Shorter connections cost some extra handshakes.

fieldGuide.symptom: Health check passes while the service is broken
causes: The check returns 200 without touching anything requests need
The fault is in a code path the check never exercises
fieldGuide.look: Error rate per instance next to health check status, and the code of the health handler.
fieldGuide.confirm: One instance shows a high 5xx rate while its health checks stay green.
fieldGuide.fix: Make readiness test resources local to the instance, such as taking a pool connection quickly. Avoid failing on a shared dependency, which would remove every instance at once.

fieldGuide.symptom: Every instance marked unhealthy at once during a brief database blip
causes: Health check depends on a dependency all instances share
fieldGuide.look: The balancer's target status timeline next to the database event.
fieldGuide.confirm: All targets turn unhealthy within one check interval of the database event.
fieldGuide.fix: Keep liveness shallow and readiness local. The cost is that some requests fail with errors during the blip instead of the balancer refusing all of them.

fieldGuide.symptom: A deploy needs five services released in a fixed order
causes: Services share a contract that cannot change compatibly
fieldGuide.look: Recent release plans and pull requests: which services changed together.
fieldGuide.confirm: The same services change in the same releases most of the time.
fieldGuide.fix: Make contract changes backward compatible, or merge services that always change together. Merging gives up independent scaling for simpler releases.

fieldGuide.symptom: Adding instances made latency and errors worse
causes: Each new instance opens more database connections
More copies send more concurrent calls to a rate-limited provider
fieldGuide.look: Database connection count and provider rate-limit headers during the scale-out.
fieldGuide.confirm: Connection errors or 429s rise in step with instance count.
fieldGuide.fix: Cap the autoscaler's maximum, put a connection pooler in front of Postgres, and size pools per instance. The cap means requests queue at the edge under extreme load.

fieldGuide.symptom: Autoscaler never adds instances while users wait
causes: Scaling on CPU for an I/O-bound service
fieldGuide.look: CPU next to in-flight requests and latency per instance during the slow period.
fieldGuide.confirm: CPU stays low while in-flight requests per instance sit at the worker limit.
fieldGuide.fix: Scale on concurrency or queue depth. These signals also rise when a dependency is slow, so cap the maximum.

fieldGuide.symptom: Scheduled email or report sent several times
causes: Every instance runs the same in-process scheduler
fieldGuide.look: Job logs grouped by instance at the scheduled minute.
fieldGuide.confirm: One run per instance, all at the same minute.
fieldGuide.fix: Run schedules in one place, or take a lock in Redis or Postgres before running. A lock must expire if its holder dies, or the job stops running.

glossary.def: Adding CPU, memory, or faster disks to one machine. Simple, with a hard ceiling and a single point of failure.
Adding more copies of a service behind a load balancer. Requires that any copy can handle any request.
A service whose processes keep nothing between requests that a later request needs. Its state lives in a database, cache, or object store.
A component that receives traffic and sends each connection or request to one healthy backend copy.
Layer 4 balancing chooses per TCP connection using addresses and ports. Layer 7 balancing reads HTTP and chooses per request.
A way to map keys to backends so that adding or removing one of N backends moves only about 1/N of the keys.
A periodic probe from the balancer or orchestrator to a backend. It proves only what the handler actually tests.
Balancer behavior that sends a user back to the same backend each time, usually by cookie. It hides local state rather than removing it.
A reverse proxy at the edge that also authenticates, rate limits, and routes requests to different services.
One deployable application with strict internal module boundaries, so modules interact only through defined interfaces.
Services that are deployed separately but must change and release together, paying the costs of microservices without their independence.
The mechanism that tells a service the current addresses of another, such as a DNS name in front of changing instances.
The average number of items in a system equals arrival rate times average time in the system. 350 requests per second lasting 7 seconds means about 2,450 open.
A rough calculation from stated assumptions to orders of magnitude, used to find the bottleneck before building anything.

apply.title: Put numbers on your own project's design
steps: Write down your project's busiest realistic day: users or runs, LLM calls per user or run, and average input and output tokens per call.
Convert that to peak calls per second (daily total divided by 86,400, times three) and peak tokens per minute. Compare tokens per minute with the limit shown in your provider's response headers.
Time one real LLM call end to end and multiply by the peak rate to get the number of calls open at once. Compare it with your HTTP client's connection pool size or your concurrency setting.
List every piece of state your process keeps between requests: in-memory dictionaries, local files, caches, timers, generated keys. Mark each one that would break if two copies ran.

quiz.q: A web API keeps each user's session in a dictionary inside its process. A second copy is added behind a round-robin load balancer. What happens?
options: Users appear logged out whenever a request reaches the other copy
The load balancer copies session data between the two copies
Both copies read one dictionary because they run the same code
Sessions keep working until one copy runs out of memory
quiz.explain: Each process has its own memory, so a session created on one copy does not exist on the other. Round robin sends about half of each user's requests to the copy that has never seen them. Running the same code does not mean sharing memory.
why: Balancers route traffic; they do not replicate application state between backends.
Identical code still runs in separate processes with separate memory.
Memory size is unrelated; the session is missing on the other copy from the first request.

quiz.context: A chat service's clients each hold one long-lived connection to the API for as long as the app is open. During a traffic spike two new copies were added 12 minutes ago, and latency has not improved.

artifact.title: Balancer metrics per backend
artifact.code:
backend  age   open_conns  req/s  cpu   health
api-1    6h    1,840       41     22%   healthy
api-2    6h    1,795       39     21%   healthy
api-3    12m   38          3      4%    healthy
api-4    12m   41          3      4%    healthy
balancing: layer 4, round robin per new connection; no max connection lifetime

quiz.q: Why are the new copies nearly idle?
options: The new copies are failing health checks and receive no traffic
Round robin skips copies that have run for less than an hour
Existing clients keep their connections, and only new connections reach the new copies
The new copies have lower CPU limits and are being throttled
quiz.explain: A layer 4 balancer places connections, not requests. Clients connected before the scale-out stay on api-1 and api-2 until they reconnect, so only the trickle of new connections reaches api-3 and api-4. Their health is fine; they are serving a few requests per second.
why: The table shows them healthy and serving a few requests per second.
Round robin has no age rule; the new copies are getting their share of new connections.
Their CPU is at 4 percent, so nothing is being throttled; they simply have little work.

quiz.q: Relay's readiness check runs `SELECT 1` against Postgres, which all API copies share. What is the main risk of this design?
options: The extra query adds noticeable load to the shared database
A short Postgres outage takes every copy out of rotation at once
It cannot detect a process that has stopped answering HTTP
It restarts every copy whenever the query is slow
quiz.explain: Because every copy shares Postgres, one database blip fails every check at once and the front door refuses all traffic. The cheap query is not a real load concern, and a check that sends a request does notice a process that has stopped answering.
why: `SELECT 1` every few seconds per copy is negligible for Postgres.
If the process stops answering HTTP, the check request fails too, so this is detected.
A readiness check only removes a copy from rotation; restarts come from a liveness check.

quiz.context: After Relay's API moved from one instance to three, most customers are logged out within minutes of logging in. Sessions are stored in Redis under an ID carried in a signed cookie. For logged-out users the session record is still present in Redis. Two of the three instances log `SECRET_KEY not set, using a random key` at startup.
options: Redis is evicting session keys under memory pressure
Instances sign and verify session cookies with different keys
The load balancer is not configured for sticky sessions
The session TTL in Redis is shorter than expected
quiz.explain: The session records still exist, which rules out eviction and TTL. A cookie signed by one instance fails verification on an instance with a different random key, so the user looks logged out. Sticky sessions would hide this until an instance restarted; one shared secret fixes it.
why: Evicted or expired keys would be missing from Redis, and they are present.
Stickiness would mask the mismatch, and users would still be logged out whenever their instance changed.
An expired TTL would remove the record, which is still there.

quiz.context: Relay has four engineers. The order lookup, refund, and chat code change together in most releases. A proposal splits them into three services.
quiz.q: What is the strongest argument against the split?
options: Separate services cannot scale independently of each other
A request through three services cannot be traced end to end
The three services would have to use different languages
Code that changes together would need coordinated releases across a network
quiz.explain: When parts change together, splitting them produces lockstep releases and version skew, the signature of a distributed monolith. Independent scaling and tracing are both possible with services, which is why they are tempting as wrong answers.
why: Independent scaling is one of the real benefits of separate services.
Distributed tracing with a propagated request ID follows a request across services.
Services can share a language; nothing forces a different one.

quiz.context: A teammate sized an internal chat tool before choosing its infrastructure.

artifact.title: The estimate
artifact.code:
daily active users       200,000
messages per user/day    5
messages per day         1,000,000
average per second       1,000,000 / 3,600 = 278
peak (x3)                ~830 per second

quiz.q: What is wrong, and what is a better peak estimate?
options: Peak should be ten times the average, so about 2,800 per second
Messages per day are ten times too high, so peak is about 83 per second
Nothing is wrong, and 830 per second is a reasonable peak
A day has 86,400 seconds, so the average is about 12 per second and peak about 35
quiz.explain: The teammate divided a daily total by the seconds in an hour. One million over 86,400 is about 12 per second, and three times that is about 35. The error inflated the estimate by 24 times, enough to justify infrastructure the tool does not need.
why: The peak factor is an assumption to discuss, but the division by 3,600 is the real error.
200,000 users times 5 messages is 1,000,000, so the daily total is right.
Dividing by 3,600 treats the whole day's traffic as if it arrived in one hour.

quiz.context: Relay needs a job queue for triage and email. The team is small, and queuing is not part of what makes Relay valuable to customers.
quiz.q: Which choice follows the build-or-buy reasoning from this day?
options: Write a broker tailored to Relay's jobs, since only a custom one fits exactly
Run triage inside each request so there is nothing to build or buy
Use a managed queue or a standard broker and spend effort on the agent
Write the queue in a faster language than Python before launch
quiz.explain: A queue is a solved problem and not Relay's advantage, so buying or adopting a standard one frees the team for the agent. Moving triage into the request avoids a dependency but puts slow work on the user's wait, which is why queues exist.
why: Custom infrastructure makes the team own every outage of a component that is not its advantage.
Running slow triage inside the request makes users wait and loses retries.
Language speed is not the constraint; the cost is building and operating the queue at all.

quiz.q: Which of these must move out of the process before Relay's API can run as several interchangeable copies? Select all that apply.
options: Session data kept in a module-level dictionary
Screenshots saved to the server's local disk
A timer that sends the nightly summary email
The FastAPI route definitions
The database URL read from an environment variable
A signing key generated randomly at startup
quiz.explain: Sessions, local files, in-process timers, and random startup keys all differ or duplicate between copies. Route definitions are code, identical in every copy, and an environment variable set the same way everywhere is configuration, not state.

quiz.q: Which of these are signs of a distributed monolith? Select all that apply.
options: Releases of several services must happen in a fixed order
Two services read and write the same database tables
Most pull requests touch code in three services at once
Each service has its own on-call rotation
Services talk through versioned, backward-compatible APIs
quiz.explain: Ordered releases, shared tables, and changes that always span services all show that the parts cannot change independently. Separate on-call and versioned compatible APIs are signs of healthy independence, the goal of splitting in the first place.

quiz.q: Put the steps of a design walkthrough in order.
items: State the requirements and the latency and retention targets
Estimate requests per second, concurrency, tokens, and storage
Draw the data path of the main request
Find the resource that saturates first
Make the choice at each step and name its cost
quiz.explain: Numbers come from requirements, the data path shows where those numbers land, and the bottleneck is visible only once both exist. Choosing components first is the memorized-answer trap, because nothing yet says which choices matter.

quiz.q: Match each observation to its most likely cause.
pairs: Logged out when a request hits another copy
Session kept in one process's memory
Each copy runs its own scheduler
New copies idle after a scale-out
Long-lived connections stay on the old copies
One copy errors while its health check is green
The health handler tests nothing that requests need
Releases need a fixed order across services
A service boundary splits one workflow
quiz.explain: Each symptom follows from where state or connections live. Asking which copy served the failing request, and what that copy holds that others do not, resolves most scaling surprises.

quiz.context: For the chat product in lesson 4 (1 million daily users, 10 messages each, 2,000 input tokens per turn, peak three times average), a teammate proposes sending the full conversation history on every turn and dropping the running summary.
quiz.q: Explain how you would evaluate the proposal.
rubric: Notes that input tokens grow with conversation length, so long conversations cost far more per turn
Checks the new peak tokens per minute against the provider's rate limit
Names the effects on cost and time to first token
Proposes measuring answer quality with an eval before and after, rather than assuming full history is better
States the tradeoff and an alternative such as prompt caching or a longer recent window
quiz.model: Full history makes input tokens grow with conversation length, so long chats cost far more per turn than the 2,000 token average. I would recompute peak input tokens per second from the real length distribution and compare it with the provider's limit, then estimate the cost and time-to-first-token change. I would run the eval set with both versions, and only accept the change if quality rises enough to pay for it, perhaps with prompt caching or a longer recent window instead.

drills.title: Logged out at random after the scale-out
drills.brief: Since Tuesday, support has received complaints that Relay logs customers out mid-conversation, sometimes twice in a minute. On Tuesday morning the team turned on autoscaling for the API, which now runs between two and six instances. Sessions are stored in Redis under a session ID carried in a signed cookie. Nobody changed the login code.

artifact.title: API access log, one customer
artifact.code:
10:14:02 POST /chat/send     200 user=u_381
10:14:09 POST /chat/send     401 user=- reason=no_session
10:14:11 GET  /chat/history  200 user=u_381
10:14:15 POST /chat/send     401 user=- reason=no_session
10:14:20 POST /chat/send     200 user=u_381

steps.q: The same cookie succeeds and fails within seconds. What do you check first?
options: Raise the session TTL in Redis to 24 hours
Group the unexpected 401s by the instance that served them
Turn on sticky sessions at the load balancer
Read the login code for a recent bug
steps.explain: A cookie that works, fails, and works again within seconds points at whatever differs between requests, and the serving instance is the obvious candidate. Splitting by instance is one query. Changing the TTL or turning on stickiness is a fix for a cause you have not found, and the login code did not change.
steps.reveal: Most unexpected 401s come from the two instances the autoscaler created since Tuesday. The two older instances serve a few hundred, and served none before Tuesday.

artifact.title: Unexpected 401s by instance, last hour
artifact.code:
instance   created          requests   unexpected_401
api-a7     2 weeks ago      9,120      412
api-b4     2 weeks ago      8,977      398
api-c2     Tue 09:12        8,640      2,911
api-f9     Tue 11:40        8,702      2,958

steps.q: Which explanation fits this pattern, and what would confirm it?
options: Redis evicts session keys; check the eviction counter in Redis
The new instances run slower; compare their latency with the old ones
The new instances verify cookies with a different key; compare their startup configuration
The balancer strips cookies for new instances; capture headers at nginx
steps.explain: Eviction would hit sessions regardless of which instance asks, so it cannot explain a clean split by instance. A difference in how new instances verify cookies matches the pattern exactly, and startup configuration is where that difference would live.
steps.reveal: The session record for a logged-out customer is still in Redis. Both new instances log a warning at startup. The autoscaler's launch template was copied from an old one that never set `SECRET_KEY`.

artifact.title: api-c2 startup
artifact.code:
09:12:31 WARNING config: SECRET_KEY not set, generating a temporary random key
09:12:31 INFO    uvicorn: Application startup complete.

options: Turn on sticky sessions so each user stays on the instance that signed the cookie
Load one signing secret from the secret manager on every instance, and refuse to start without it
Keep sessions in each instance's memory to avoid the Redis lookup
Turn autoscaling off and return to the two original instances
steps.explain: A shared secret lets any instance verify any cookie, and refusing to start turns a silent misconfiguration into a loud failed launch. Sticky sessions would still log users out whenever their instance is replaced, and disabling autoscaling removes the capacity the team needed.
steps.reveal: With the shared secret in the launch template, unexpected 401s drop to zero on all instances.

steps.q: The fix is live. What else is worth checking before closing this?
options: Whether Redis needs more memory for sessions
Whether round robin should become least connections
Whether the login page loads faster with the new key
Whether any other setting differs between the old and new launch configuration
steps.explain: A copied template that missed one variable may have missed others, such as a log level, a feature flag, or a pool size. Diffing the two configurations is cheap. Redis memory and the balancing algorithm have nothing to do with the evidence.
steps.reveal: The diff also shows the new template sets a smaller database pool than the old instances use. It is corrected in the same change.

drills.debrief: Root cause: instances launched by the new autoscaler lacked `SECRET_KEY`, so each generated its own random key, rejected cookies signed elsewhere, and issued cookies that every other instance rejected. The plausible wrong cause, Redis eviction, was ruled out because the session records still existed and the failures split cleanly by instance. Fail fast on missing secrets, keep one template, and test a scale-out before relying on it. The general lesson: when behavior depends on which copy served the request, look for state or config that differs between copies.

drills.title: One copy fails while its health check stays green
drills.brief: At 14:20 Relay's error rate rose from under 0.1 percent to about 25 percent and has held there for 40 minutes. Customers see 'Something went wrong' on about one message in four. The load balancer reports all four API instances healthy. Postgres dashboards look normal. A deploy went out at 13:05.

options: Roll back the 13:05 deploy
Break down the 5xx responses by instance
Fail Postgres over to the replica
Restart all four API instances
steps.explain: An error rate stuck near 25 percent with four instances suggests one instance failing everything. The breakdown takes a minute and tells you whether the problem is the build, the database, or one copy. Rolling back or restarting first would destroy that evidence.
steps.reveal: Almost every 5xx comes from api-3. All four instances run the same build, and the other three are serving normally.

artifact.title: Last 30 minutes by instance
artifact.code:
instance  build    requests  5xx    health
api-1     4f2a91   6,912     3      healthy
api-2     4f2a91   6,870     2      healthy
api-3     4f2a91   6,955     6,931  healthy
api-4     4f2a91   6,898     4      healthy

steps.q: The build is the same everywhere. What do you read next?
options: The diff of the 13:05 deploy
The Postgres slow query log
The application logs of api-3
The load balancer's TLS settings
steps.explain: The fault is local to one instance running the same code as healthy ones, so that instance's own logs are the cheapest evidence. The deploy diff is the same for all four, and Postgres is serving the other three normally.
steps.reveal: Each failing request waits 30 seconds for a database connection and gives up. Meanwhile the health check answers 200 in a millisecond. In Postgres, `pg_stat_activity` shows ten connections from api-3 in state `idle in transaction` since 14:19.

artifact.title: api-3
artifact.code:
14:52:10 ERROR POST /chat/send sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError: QueuePool limit of size 10
         overflow 0 reached, connection timed out, timeout 30.00
14:52:11 INFO  GET /healthz 200 1ms

steps.q: Why does the load balancer keep sending traffic to api-3?
options: The balancer uses sticky sessions for api-3's users
The health check interval is too long to notice
The balancer works at layer 4 and cannot see HTTP errors
The health handler returns 200 without taking a pool connection
steps.explain: The check has been passing for 40 minutes, so interval length is irrelevant. It passes because the handler never touches the exhausted pool. The balancer is doing exactly what the check tells it, and the check tests nothing that requests need.
steps.reveal: The `/healthz` handler returns a constant response. It is used for both liveness and readiness.

steps.q: What do you do now, and what afterwards?
options: Drain and restart api-3 now, then find the code path that leaves transactions open
Make the health check query Postgres on every instance, then restart api-3
Raise api-3's pool size to 50 and leave it running
Roll back all instances to the previous build, then investigate
steps.explain: Restarting api-3 releases its stuck connections and stops a quarter of requests failing. Then the leak needs finding, because it will recur. A shared-dependency health check would turn the next database blip into a full outage, and a larger pool only delays exhaustion. A rollback is not indicated, since three instances run the same build without errors.
steps.reveal: After the restart, errors return to baseline. The code review finds that the `issue_refund` tool handler skips its rollback when the payment provider times out. The provider had a brief slowdown at 14:19.

drills.debrief: Root cause: a refund handler leaked a database transaction whenever the payment provider timed out. During a short provider slowdown api-3 leaked all ten of its connections, and its constant health check kept it in rotation. Fix the leak with a transaction scope that always closes, make readiness take a pool connection with a short timeout, and alert on per-instance error rate. Check the other instances' `idle in transaction` counts, since they may have leaked some connections too. The general lesson: a health check proves only what it tests.
